blocks.text: You shall trample the poisonous dragon and the lion under your feet. And Leo Africanus, book 9: [III, 237] The dragons of Atlas are extremely poisonous: and if by chance they either touch or bite anyone, they soften and weaken the flesh. Indeed in Africa and Numidia all serpents have a more deadly poison than in other lands. Hence Horace, book 3, Ode 10,
And at the end of book 2 of the Satires,
— — — — as if Canidia had breathed on them, worse than African serpents.

Everyone knows that serpents are extremely fond of wine. For the Philosopher teaches this in History, book 8, chapter 4: Οἱ δὲ ὄφεις καὶ πρὸς τὸν οἶνόν εἰσιν ἀκρατοὺς. Διὸ θηρεύουσί τινες καὶ τοὺς ἔχεις εἰς ὀστράκια, διὰ τὸ τιθέναι οἶνον εἰς τὰς αἱμασίας· λαμβάνονται γὰρ μεθύοντες. [Hoi de opheis kai pros ton oinon eisin akratous. Dio thēreuousi tines kai tous echeis eis ostrakia, dia to tithenai oinon eis tas haimasias; lambanontai gar methyontes.] Serpents are greedy for wine. Accordingly some hunt vipers by setting out wine in earthenware vessels by the hedges: for they are caught drunk. And Pliny, book 10, chapter 72: Serpents, when there is opportunity, especially crave wine. But that by drinking wine the poison of serpents and dragons becomes sharper and stronger I have learned from no other source than the Chaldee Jonathan, who, for the words of Moses, The poison of dragons is their poison, Deut. XXXII, 33, has this in his Paraphrase: הי כמרירתהון דתניניא כי הנך הוון מן חמרהון בגין כן יהי מריר כס דלוות דישתון ביום פורענותהון, Behold! as is the gall of dragons when they are from their wine (that is, after they have drunk wine), so shall be the gall of the cup from which they shall drink on the day of their punishment.

The dragon seeks out solitary places, τὴν ἐρημίαν πρὸ τῶν ἀστικῶν διατριβῶν [tēn erēmian pro tōn astikōn diatribōn], says Aelian, book 6, chapter 63. Plutarch therefore acutely denies, in his book On the Obsolescence of Oracles, that what they say is true, that Delphi was once deserted because a dragon lived there; rather, the dragon lived there because the place was deserted. Ἡ γὰρ ἐρημία τὸ θηρίον ἐπηγάγετο, μᾶλλον ἢ τὸ θηρίον ἐποίησε τὴν ἐρημίαν. [Hē gar erēmia to thērion epēgageto, mallon ē to thērion epoiēse tēn erēmian.] This is why the Prophets so often ^{b)} foretell that the most populous cities will become the dwellings of dragons, or will be inhabited by dragons. By these words they threaten them with utter desolation. So Aquila rendered not badly at Ps. XLIV, 20: You have crushed us ἐν τόπῳ ἀοικήτῳ [en topō aoikētō], in an uninhabitable place, for what is in Hebrew in the place of dragons. But although dragons often live in thirsty places, yet, where they are free to choose, they settle much more gladly in well-watered valleys. Thus also of real dragons, in its own [col. 439] [III, 238] way, what Isaiah ^{c)} prophesied of mystical dragons, that is, of the nations far from the knowledge of the true God but to be called in due time, is true: that the dragons will glorify God, when he has put waters in the desert and rivers in the wilderness. And in Nehem. II, 13. the dragon's spring near Jerusalem seems to be named from a dragon that used to lurk there while the city lay desolate. So Pausanias in his Boeotica describes a spring near the river Ismenus, over which a dragon was set as guardian, by Mars, of course. And Philostratus, book 3, chapter 2, observes that Homer placed the dragon at Aulis by a spring, περὶ κρήνην [peri krēnēn]. This is far more probable than what Villalpandus conjectures, that this little spring nourished those large fish which in Hebrew are called תנים. But it also seems forced, what a learned man asserts, that the spring of Siloam is named from its slow and creeping flow, of which Es. VIII, 6. The Greeks render πηγὴν τῶν συκῶν [pēgēn tōn sykōn], the spring of the figs, because for תנים they read תאנים. The Syriac, however, has ܥܝܢܐ ܕܬܠܠܐ, the spring of the hills, as if it had read תלים.

In Apocal. XII, 9. the devil is called the great dragon and the ancient serpent, which come to almost the same thing. For it is reported that serpents, over a long course of years, at length become dragons. Moreover, not just any demon is called dragon, but the one who seduced Eve. Most hold, further, that he is the prince of demons, and that the name dragon signifies that he is as eminent among the demons as a great dragon is among the common run of serpents. Accordingly Philo Judaeus ^{d)}, who wrote before John, also calls this very demon a dragon. Ταῦτα δὲ, he says, οὕτω μὲν λεγόμενα φάσμασιν ἔοικε, καὶ τέρασι, δράκων ἀνθρώπου προϊέμενος φωνὴν, καὶ ἐνσοφιστεύων ἀκακωτάτοις ἤθεσι, καὶ πιθανότησιν εὐπαραγώγοις γυναῖκα ἀπατῶν· [Tauta de ... houtō men legomena phasmasin eoike, kai terasi, drakōn anthrōpou proiemenos phōnēn, kai ensophisteuōn akakōtatois ēthesi, kai pithanotēsin euparagōgois gynaika apatōn;] These things, as they are related, might seem closer to apparitions and portents: a dragon uttering human [col. 440] words, and corrupting the most innocent character with subtleties, and deceiving the woman with persuasions by which she is easily imposed upon. The Hebrews too call him הנחש הקדמוני, the ancient serpent. This was observed long ago by Drusius on this passage, and by Paulus Fagius on Genesis. Nor is the reason for the name obscure.
